title: Explain the Kubernetes architecture — control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) and worker nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime) — and how the scheduler decides where to place a pod.
shortTitle: Kubernetes Architecture — Control Plane, Worker Nodes, and How the Scheduler Places a Pod

s1_definition.profdef: Kubernetes has two planes. The control plane is the brain: the API server is the single front door that validates and stores all requests, etcd is the consistent key-value store holding the entire cluster state, the scheduler decides which worker node each new pod should run on, and the controller manager runs control loops that continuously drive the actual state toward the desired state. The worker nodes run the workloads: the kubelet on each node ensures its assigned pods are running and healthy, kube-proxy programs the networking rules so services are reachable, and the container runtime (such as containerd) actually pulls images and runs containers. The scheduler places a pod by first filtering nodes that can run it (fit) and then scoring the remaining nodes to pick the best one.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's head office and its branches. The control plane is head office: the API server is the reception desk that is the only way to submit any request and checks it is valid; etcd is the master ledger recording the authoritative state of everything; the scheduler is the staffing planner who decides which branch a new employee should be posted to; and the controller manager is the operations team constantly comparing "how many staff should each branch have" to "how many it actually has" and hiring or moving people to close the gap. The worker nodes are the branches: the kubelet is the branch manager making sure the posted staff actually show up and do their jobs, kube-proxy is the internal phone directory routing calls to the right desk, and the container runtime is the facilities team that physically sets up each workstation. The staffing planner posts a new employee by first ruling out branches that cannot host them and then picking the best remaining branch.

**Professional definition:** Kubernetes has two planes. The control plane is the brain: the API server is the single front door that validates and stores all requests, etcd is the consistent key-value store holding the entire cluster state, the scheduler decides which worker node each new pod should run on, and the controller manager runs control loops that continuously drive the actual state toward the desired state. The scheduler places a pod by first filtering nodes that can run it (fit) and then scoring the remaining nodes to pick the best one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's head office and its branches. The control plane is head office: the API server is the reception desk that is the only way to submit any request and checks it is valid; etcd is the master ledger recording the authoritative state of everything; the scheduler is the staffing planner who decides which branch a new employee should be posted to; and the controller manager is the operations team constantly comparing "how many staff should each branch have" to "how many it actually has" and hiring or moving people to close the gap. The worker nodes are the branches: the kubelet is the branch manager making sure the posted staff actually show up and do their jobs, kube-proxy is the internal phone directory routing calls to the right desk, and the container runtime is the facilities team that physically sets up each workstation. The staffing planner posts a new employee by first ruling out branches that cannot host them and then picking the best remaining branch.

**One line to remember:** The control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) decides and records desired state, the worker nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy, runtime) run the workloads, and the scheduler places a pod by filtering nodes that fit then scoring them to pick the best.

sections.s2_technical:
The API server is the hub of the control plane. Every interaction, whether from kubectl, a controller, or the kubelet, goes through the API server, which authenticates, authorises, validates, and then persists the object. Nothing talks to etcd directly except the API server, which keeps a single, consistent entry point and enforces access control in one place.

etcd is the cluster's source of truth. It is a distributed, strongly consistent key-value store holding the entire desired and observed state: every deployment, pod spec, config map, and secret reference. If etcd is lost, the cluster's memory is lost, which is why in banking it is run as an odd-numbered quorum with regular backups and encryption at rest.

The scheduler assigns pods to nodes. When a pod is created with no node assigned, the scheduler watches for it and decides placement. The controller manager runs the control loops: for example the deployment and replicaset controllers ensure the right number of pod replicas exist, and the node controller reacts to nodes going unhealthy. Each controller continuously compares desired state in etcd to observed state and takes corrective action, which is the reconciliation pattern at the heart of Kubernetes.

On each worker node the kubelet is the agent that makes reality match the spec. It watches the API server for pods assigned to its node, tells the container runtime to pull images and start containers, runs the liveness and readiness probes, and reports status back. Kube-proxy programs the node's networking (iptables or IPVS rules) so that traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced to the right pod endpoints. The container runtime, commonly containerd, is what actually runs containers via the CRI interface.

The scheduling decision is a two-phase process: filtering then scoring. In filtering (also called predicates), the scheduler eliminates nodes that cannot run the pod: nodes without enough free CPU or memory for the pod's requests, nodes whose taints the pod does not tolerate, nodes that do not match the pod's node selector or required affinity, and nodes that cannot satisfy volume or port constraints. In scoring (also called priorities), each surviving node gets a score based on factors like how well the pod's requests fit the node's remaining resources, spreading pods of the same workload across nodes and zones for resilience, and affinity preferences. The scheduler picks the highest-scoring node and binds the pod to it, after which that node's kubelet starts it.

A senior nuance is that you influence placement deliberately in banking: taints and tolerations keep general workloads off dedicated nodes (for example a node pool reserved for sensitive payment services), node affinity pins workloads to zones or hardware, pod anti-affinity spreads replicas so one node failure does not take down a whole service, and topology spread constraints balance across availability zones for resilience. Another nuance is resource requests versus limits: requests drive scheduling (the scheduler reserves based on requests) while limits cap runtime usage, so setting requests too low overcommits a node and setting them too high wastes capacity. A third nuance is that the control plane itself is made highly available with multiple API server replicas and an etcd quorum, because for a banking cluster the control plane going down means you cannot deploy or self-heal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs to run many copies of the transfer service, and someone must decide which machine each copy runs on so no machine is overloaded and copies are spread for resilience. This is exactly the job of the scheduler. It filters nodes that have room and then scores them to spread replicas.

Problem 2 — Sensitive payment-processing pods must never land on general-purpose nodes shared with less-trusted workloads. This is exactly the problem taints and tolerations plus node affinity solve. The payment node pool is tainted so only pods that tolerate it and are affined to it can be placed there.

Problem 3 — If all three replicas of the transfer service landed on one node and that node died, the service would be fully down. This is exactly the problem anti-affinity and topology spread solve. The scheduler spreads replicas across nodes and zones.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation of the scheduler's two-phase decision. We will model a `Node` with capacity, taints, and a zone; a `PodSpec` with resource requests, tolerations, and a spread preference; a `Scheduler` that filters nodes that fit and then scores the survivors; and we will schedule several transfer-service replicas plus a sensitive payment pod to show filtering (payment pod only fits the tainted payment node) and scoring (replicas spread across zones). This mirrors the real filter-then-score placement.

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.k8s.SchedulerDemo

# Real cluster inspection:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node node-a                 # capacity, taints, allocatable
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three nodes (two general-purpose in zones 1 and 2, and one tainted "payments" node in zone 1) and four pods (three transfer replicas that want spreading, and one sensitive payment pod).

Step 1: The first transfer replica is scheduled. Filtering keeps the two general nodes (node-a and node-b) and rejects the tainted node-c because the replica does not tolerate the payments taint. Scoring favours a node not yet holding this workload; both are empty, so it picks one, say node-a in zone 1, and places the pod, reducing node-a's free resources and incrementing its workload count.

Step 2: The second replica is scheduled. Filtering again keeps node-a and node-b. Scoring now penalises node-a because it already holds one replica of this workload, so node-b in zone 2 scores higher and is chosen, spreading the two replicas across two zones for resilience.

Step 3: The third replica is scheduled. Both node-a and node-b now hold one replica each, so scoring is closer, and whichever has more free resources or fewer workload pods wins, placing the third replica to keep the spread as balanced as possible. The tainted node-c is still excluded throughout.

Step 4: The sensitive payment pod is scheduled. It tolerates the payments taint, so filtering now keeps node-c (and would keep the general nodes too), but the key point is that only the payment pod can use node-c because only it tolerates the taint. The transfer replicas never landed there, keeping sensitive and general workloads separated.

Step 5: Across all four, filtering enforced the hard constraints (resources and taints) and scoring expressed the soft preference (spread), which is exactly the two-phase decision the real scheduler makes, and the result is balanced, resilient, and correctly isolated placement.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  kubectl apply (pod with no node)
    │
    ▼
  API Server ──validate/auth──▶ etcd (store desired state)
    │ scheduler watches for unassigned pods
    ▼
  SCHEDULER
    ├─ Phase 1 FILTER (predicates)
    │    node resources fit? taint tolerated? selector/affinity match?
    │    → feasible nodes
    ▼
    ├─ Phase 2 SCORE (priorities)
    │    balanced fit + spread (anti-affinity/topology) + preferences
    │    → best node
    ▼
  Bind pod → node   (written back via API Server → etcd)
    │
    ▼
  kubelet on that node ──▶ container runtime pulls image, runs container
                       └─▶ probes report health; kube-proxy routes service traffic
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes splits into a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane is the brain. The API server is the single front door that authenticates, authorises, validates, and persists every request, and nothing talks to the datastore except through it. etcd is the strongly consistent key-value store that holds the entire desired and observed state, so it is the cluster's source of truth and in banking is run as an odd-numbered quorum with backups and encryption. The scheduler decides which node each new pod runs on. The controller manager runs the reconciliation loops, such as the deployment and replicaset controllers that keep the right number of replicas and the node controller that reacts to unhealthy nodes, each continuously driving actual state toward desired state.

The worker nodes run the workloads. The kubelet is the per-node agent that watches the API server for pods assigned to its node, tells the container runtime to pull images and start containers, runs the liveness and readiness probes, and reports status back. Kube-proxy programs the node's networking so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced to the right pods. The container runtime, usually containerd, actually runs the containers.

The scheduler places a pod in two phases. First it filters, eliminating nodes that cannot run the pod because they lack enough CPU or memory for the pod's requests, carry a taint the pod does not tolerate, or fail a node selector or affinity or volume constraint. Then it scores the surviving nodes on factors like how well the requests fit the remaining resources and how well placement spreads replicas across nodes and zones, and it binds the pod to the highest-scoring node, after which that node's kubelet starts it.

On the banking project I used this directly. The transfer service ran three replicas, and I used topology spread constraints and pod anti-affinity so the scheduler placed them across different nodes and availability zones, so one node or zone failure could never take the whole service down. Sensitive payment-processing pods ran on a dedicated node pool that was tainted, with the payment pods given the matching toleration and node affinity, so general workloads could never be scheduled onto those nodes. The senior points I always add are that resource requests drive scheduling while limits cap runtime, so getting requests right is essential to avoid overcommitting or wasting a node, and that the control plane itself must be highly available with multiple API server replicas and an etcd quorum, because for a banking cluster a control-plane outage means you can neither deploy nor self-heal.
